case_study_insert.main_stem: Paloma Rose Boutique (PRB) is a private limited company in the occasionwear retail sector, based in San Antonio, Texas, employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2014 by Paloma Rivera, it runs three boutiques selling dresses and occasionwear and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. PRB plans to invest $650,000 in a fourth boutique in Austin with an online style-advice service, financed by $400,000 venture capital and $250,000 retained profit. The business has fixed costs of $420,000 a year, a variable cost of $17.00 a unit and a selling price of $38.00, and currently produces 32,000 units a year. PRB faces high labour turnover, with 22% of seasonal staff leaving before the festive season.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Advertisement Extract — 'Spring Occasionwear 2026' campaign (6 weeks, Instagram and print): Reach 210,000; 8,400 clicks, a 4.0% click-through rate; 1,950 orders placed; 640 orders (32.8%) used voucher code SPRING26; average order value $86; campaign cost $24,500, a cost of $12.56 per order; and 1,320 campaign-driven store visits were logged at the tills.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Paloma Rose Boutique as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate to 6.0%, the highest since 2008, increasing borrowing costs for retailers on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will increase by 5.6% from $13.00 to $13.73 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills across retail. (3) High-street retail rents rose 9.4% year-on-year and PRB's landlord has quoted a 9.4% increase for the proposed Austin premises, adding an estimated $42,000 a year, while consumer spending on occasionwear grew 4.8%.

questions.question_text: PRB plans to fund the Austin boutique with venture capital and retained profit. Explain two advantages for PRB of using venture capital to fund the expansion instead of a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Venture capital arrives as equity, not debt, so PRB carries no interest charge and no fixed monthly repayments while the Austin store establishes its customer base. This protects the cash flow needed for the festive peak, avoids the risk of default that a loan would carry, and leaves the $250,000 retained profit untouched as a cushion against the 22% labour turnover and the 9.4% rent increase quoted for the premises.

Point 2: Venture capital investors in retail typically bring more than money: site-selection experience, supplier introductions and marketing know-how that can accelerate the Austin launch and the online style-advice service, shortening the time before the new boutique contributes towards the $420,000 annual fixed costs. Unlike a bank, which is indifferent to success beyond repayment, the investor's return depends on growth, so both parties are aligned. Crucially, PRB is not exposed to the 6.0% base rate on this capital, which keeps financing costs predictable while occasionwear consumer spending grows 4.8% a year and competition for the Austin site intensifies.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to PRB's expansion, finance choices, labour turnover and the Austin rent quote.

questions.question_text: PRB is opening its fourth boutique in Austin. Consider billboard hoardings across Austin, local radio sponsorship or social media influencer marketing to promote the opening. Which should PRB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Billboard hoardings: Large hoardings on Austin commuter routes would give the new boutique broad local visibility with repeated daily impressions. They suit a single catchment and build recognition fast. However, they are expensive to rent and print, cannot be targeted to occasionwear buyers specifically, and provide no direct response data — unlike the voucher code that tracked 1,320 store visits and 640 redemptions in the spring campaign — so PRB cannot tell whether the spend drives footfall or merely awareness.

Local radio sponsorship: Sponsoring an Austin drive-time or lifestyle show reaches exactly the car-commuting, style-conscious audience most likely to visit, and the station can voice a repeating opening offer with voucher code mechanics for measurement at a fraction of hoarding cost. It suits a flat, laissez-faire boutique where the creative team can script the spots. Weaknesses are limited reach beyond the metro area and no visual presence for fashion, though window displays and in-store styling can carry the visual side.

Social media influencer marketing: Austin fashion and lifestyle influencers could model occasionwear to younger followers, extending the 4.0% click-through behaviour of the spring campaign. However, influencer fees are paid regardless of results, audiences skew to followers living outside Austin, and attribution for a single-store opening is murky at best.

Recommendation: PRB should choose local radio sponsorship. It is the cheapest option delivering repeated, measurable, locally concentrated exposure carrying a redemption code, it fits a launch that must fill a new boutique quickly, and it avoids heavy fixed costs on a business whose fixed costs already run at $420,000 a year. Billboards are rejected as costly and unmeasurable for a data-driven business with proven voucher redemption, influencer marketing is rejected as untargeted for a single-city opening, with social promotion kept only as a supporting tactic.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the three promotional options with minimal application to PRB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of PRB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of PRB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why hoardings and influencer marketing are rejected.

questions.question_text: PRB's labour turnover among seasonal staff has reached 22% before the festive season. Explain two benefits for PRB of using laissez-faire leadership to improve motivation in its boutique team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership gives experienced occasionwear consultants genuine autonomy over styling, merchandising and clienteling, satisfying their esteem and self-actualisation needs (Maslow). Staff who feel trusted are more loyal and engaged, which directly attacks the 22% seasonal labour turnover that leaves boutiques short-staffed in the festive peak when occasionwear demand is highest.

Point 2: In a flat structure, laissez-faire leadership removes layers of sign-off, so consultants can respond instantly to clients, tailor recommendations and build the personal relationships that drive repeat purchases — reinforcing the $86 average order value PRB measured online. Creative freedom also produces fresher window displays, stronger social content and better-themed rails for the three boutiques, lifting footfall without extra cost. For seasonal staff facing the festive rush, feeling trusted rather than micromanaged is a powerful reason to stay past February, easing the 22% labour turnover and preserving client relationships built up by colleagues who leave.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to PRB's labour turnover, flat structure and festive-season trading.

questions.question_text: PRB needs seasonal shop assistants motivated for the festive rush. Consider an individual sales bonus or job rotation between departments. Which should PRB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Individual sales bonus: A bonus paid on personal sales gives each seasonal assistant a direct, immediate incentive to engage every customer, upsell accessories and convert fitting-room visits during the festive rush. It is simple to calculate from till data, repeats the incentive every shift and requires no reorganisation of the boutiques. Its drawbacks are that it can encourage pushy selling or rivalry between colleagues, may disadvantage part-time staff on quieter shifts, and does nothing to build the broader skills that would make seasonal workers worth rehiring next year.

Job rotation: Rotating assistants between the tills, shop floor, visual merchandising and the fitting room builds a multi-skilled, flexible workforce, relieves monotony and signals commitment to long-term development — valuable when 22% of seasonal staff leave early. However, rotation during the busiest trading weeks of the year risks confusion and slower service, demands training time PRB does not have in late November, and weakens individual accountability for transactions and average order value.

Decision: PRB should choose the individual sales bonus for the festive period. It is fast to introduce, measurable from till data, directly tied to the revenue PRB must generate before Christmas and it motivates exactly the temporary workers most at risk of disengaging during the busiest six weeks of the year. Job rotation is rejected for now because reshuffling inexperienced temporary staff across departments in peak weeks would damage service, erode the average value per order and overload permanent staff who must re-train colleagues; PRB can rotate its permanent team between seasons once the December rush has passed and use rotation as next year's retention lever instead.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of a bonus and job rotation with limited application to PRB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both motivation methods in the context of PRB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of PRB with a well-justified decision covering festive trading, cost and labour turnover.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how PRB's management can use its cost, break-even and safety-margin data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $420,000 ÷ ($38.00 − $17.00) = $420,000 ÷ $21.00 = 20,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 20,000 units a year.
Formula: Margin of safety = Actual output − Break-even output. Substitution: 32,000 units − 20,000 units = 12,000 units. Answer: margin of safety is 12,000 units a year.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways PRB's management can use this break-even and margin of safety data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. The margin of safety of 12,000 units shows PRB can lose up to 37.5% of annual sales before losses begin, reassuring managers that the Austin expansion will not break even only at unrealistic volume.
2. Contribution per unit of $21.00 lets managers model a 10% opening promotion (new price $34.20, contribution $17.20) to test whether festive footfall gains would still cover the $420,000 fixed costs.
3. Break-even output supports the finance review: the Austin store must sell well above 20,000 units a year to service repayments, informing whether PRB should draw down the $250,000 retained profit or stage the venture capital investment instead.
4. Unit cost data ($420,000 ÷ 32,000 units + $17.00 = $30.125, about $30.13 a unit) benchmarks each quarter, helping managers judge whether the 22% seasonal labour turnover is eroding productivity and whether prices should move above $38.00.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 20,000 units | (ii) Margin of safety = 12,000 units | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety headroom of 12,000 units; discount modelling at $21.00 contribution; feasibility of the Austin expansion financing; unit-cost benchmarking at $30.125 a unit to address labour turnover and pricing above $38.00.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate PRB's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has PRB's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.70 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.77 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.61 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.74 : 1

Detailed workings: Current assets 2024 = $380,000 inventories + $190,000 trade receivables + $25,000 cash = $595,000. Current assets 2025 = $320,000 + $170,000 + $60,000 = $550,000. Short-term cover 2024 = $595,000 ÷ $350,000 = 1.70; 2025 = $550,000 ÷ $310,000 = 1.77. Stricter measure 2024 = ($595,000 − $380,000) ÷ $350,000 = $215,000 ÷ $350,000 = 0.61; 2025 = ($550,000 − $320,000) ÷ $310,000 = $230,000 ÷ $310,000 = 0.74.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. Short-term cover rose from 1.70 to 1.77 as current liabilities fell from $350,000 to $310,000, and cash more than doubled from $25,000 to $60,000. The stricter measure improved from 0.61 to 0.74, so PRB relies much less on selling dresses to pay short-term debts — important while opening a fourth boutique costing $650,000. However, total current assets fell from $595,000 to $550,000 because inventories were deliberately cleared from $380,000 to $320,000 to reduce mark-down risk ahead of the festive season; if Austin demand proves stronger than expected, PRB may carry too little stock for peak trading. Trade receivables remain elevated at $170,000.

Conclusion: PRB's financial position has improved. The stronger cover (1.70 to 1.77) and stricter measure (0.61 to 0.74), rising cash and falling liabilities outweigh the shrinking asset base, and the improvement will support the Austin launch. PRB should keep inventory lean but sufficient for festive demand and tighten collection of receivables so the improvement is sustained into 2026.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether PRB's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PRB of expanding with a physical boutique in Austin rather than only growing online.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A physical Austin boutique lets customers try occasionwear for fit, fabric and cut — the emotional core of occasion purchases — and converts curiosity into staff-guided styling advice that online cannot replicate. In-store events, personal styling appointments and alterations lift average order values above the $86 seen online, while 1,320 campaign-driven store visits logging 640 voucher redemptions already proved local demand exists. The boutique also anchors brand presence for the new online style-advice service across the Austin catchment.

Disadvantage: A fourth boutique adds $650,000 of capital and a new stream of fixed costs on top of the $420,000 a year PRB already carries — including an Austin rent quoted 9.4% above current rates, adding an estimated $42,000 a year. Physical expansion is also hard to reverse if trends turn: online demand can be scaled quickly, whereas leases, fittings and a new local team lock up cash, complicate the exit if festive sales disappoint, and raise the fixed-cost bar every month.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to PRB's Austin plan, rent quote, campaign data and fixed costs.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 6.0%, the 5.6% minimum wage increase to $13.73 and the 9.4% rent increase will affect PRB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (to 6.0%): PRB expanded with venture capital and retained profit rather than debt, so direct interest exposure is minimal — unlike highly indebted rivals, PRB has no variable-rate loan on the expansion. Higher rates may raise lease financing costs and cool occasionwear demand slightly, but this is the smallest of the three impacts, and any overdraft can be managed through retaining the $60,000 cash balance PRB built in 2025.

Minimum wage increase (5.6%, to $13.73 per hour): Retail employs high proportions of minimum-wage staff. The 5.6% rise is a certain, permanent increase in staffing costs that laissez-faire leadership and productivity must absorb, likely squeezing payroll budgets or forcing selective price rises above the $38.00 average.

Rent increase (9.4%, adding an estimated $42,000 a year on the proposed Austin premises): This lands directly on the new store's profitability and on PRB's $420,000 fixed-cost base. It is specific, quantified by the landlord and unavoidable if PRB signs the lease — but it is concentrated on one site and potentially negotiable, unlike a wage bill spread across all 48 staff.

Conclusion: The 5.6% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It applies broadly across retail's minimum-wage workforce and recurs every year, while the Austin rent exposure is specific and potentially negotiable and the interest-rate rise is a future risk PRB has largely avoided by funding growth with venture capital and retained profit. PRB must offset the wage rise through scheduling efficiency, cross-training and modest price rises while keeping its debt-free funding model.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to PRB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on PRB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of PRB with a well-justified judgment that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
